rows.source: UKHSA giardiasis guidance and surveillance
rows.verified: Giardia is an intestinal parasite of humans and animals that can cause giardiasis.

rows.source: UKHSA giardiasis guidance and surveillance
rows.verified: Diarrhoea is the most common giardiasis symptom, with cramps, bloating and flatulence also reported.

rows.source: UKHSA giardiasis guidance and surveillance
rows.verified: Giardiasis can spread through direct contact with infected humans or animals.

rows.source: UKHSA giardiasis guidance and surveillance
rows.verified: Contaminated food, water or beverages can transmit Giardia.

rows.source: UKHSA giardiasis guidance and surveillance
rows.verified: Swimming in contaminated lakes, rivers or other water can result in infection.

rows.source: UKHSA giardiasis guidance and surveillance
rows.verified: Many giardiasis cases are associated with foreign travel.

rows.source: UKHSA giardiasis guidance and surveillance
rows.verified: The reported incubation period for giardiasis is 5 to 25 days.

rows.source: UKHSA giardiasis guidance and surveillance
rows.verified: In children's settings, handwashing, enhanced cleaning and temporary exclusion from swimming are recommended controls after giardiasis.

rows.source: UKHSA giardiasis guidance and surveillance
rows.verified: Giardiasis risk depends on water and food quality, animal or human contact, travel, swimming exposure, hygiene, immunity and timing.

rows.source: UKHSA giardiasis guidance and surveillance
rows.verified: UKHSA Giardia evidence is pathogen-, exposure-, traveller-, setting-, patient- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.

rows.source: UKHSA scabies case and outbreak management
rows.verified: UKHSA scabies guidance covers care homes, boarding schools, children's homes, detention settings, asylum accommodation and homeless hostels.

rows.source: UKHSA scabies case and outbreak management
rows.verified: Diagnosed scabies cases should be treated promptly rather than waiting for wider setting treatment.

rows.source: UKHSA scabies case and outbreak management
rows.verified: Close contacts during the 8 weeks before diagnosis should be identified, including relevant visitors.

rows.source: UKHSA scabies case and outbreak management
rows.verified: Treatment of identified contacts should be coordinated to break the transmission cycle.

rows.source: UKHSA scabies case and outbreak management
rows.verified: Two or more epidemiologically linked cases in one setting within 8 weeks constitute an outbreak.

rows.source: UKHSA scabies case and outbreak management
rows.verified: Outbreak controls include suitable PPE, cleaning, laundry management, visitor information and transfer risk assessment.

rows.source: UKHSA scabies case and outbreak management
rows.verified: A person with scabies is considered infectious until 24 hours after the first treatment dose.

rows.source: UKHSA scabies case and outbreak management
rows.verified: Scabies is primarily spread by close skin-to-skin contact, while crusted scabies presents greater onward-transmission risk.

rows.source: UKHSA scabies case and outbreak management
rows.verified: Scabies risk depends on case type, skin contact, setting, crowding, personal care, diagnosis delay, coordinated treatment and cleaning.

rows.source: UKHSA scabies case and outbreak management
rows.verified: UKHSA scabies evidence is case-, contact-, setting-, treatment-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infestation probability.
